title: Zechariah 3:1–10
context: Zechariah 3:1–10 is commonly counted as the fourth of eight night visions (1:7–6:8) that the prophet Zechariah received in the second year of Darius (1:7), though some readers set it apart because its form differs from the others. In those years Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest led the returned community in rebuilding the temple (Haggai 1:1, 14; Ezra 5:1–2). The prophet sees Joshua standing before the LORD’s angel, with Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary (3:1). Readers in both traditions identify the angel of the LORD in different ways, some seeing a created angel and others an appearance of the Son before the incarnation, and these notes hold those readings side by side. The Hebrew noun satan means adversary or accuser, and here it carries the definite article. Readers take the figure as a heavenly accuser or prosecutor in the LORD’s court, as in Job 1–2, or as Satan in the fuller sense that later Christian readers find in passages such as Revelation 12:10, and some hold the two together; the text itself does not settle the question. On how God’s rule relates to hostile agents, see the Judges 9:23 box. The LORD rebukes the accuser and calls Joshua “a burning stick plucked out of the fire”, the same image Amos 4:11 uses for Israel (3:2). Joshua’s filthy garments are removed and replaced with rich clothing, the angel declares his iniquity taken away, and the prophet himself asks for a clean turban (3:3–5). The LORD’s angel then gives Joshua a charge with conditions: if he walks in the LORD’s ways and follows his instructions, he will judge the LORD’s house, keep his courts, and have access among those who stand by (3:6–7). The LORD of Armies promises to bring “my servant, the Branch” (3:8), speaks of a stone with seven eyes set before Joshua and of removing “the iniquity of that land in one day” (3:9), and closes with neighbors invited under vine and fig tree (3:10; compare Micah 4:4 and 1 Kings 4:25). The Branch draws on the Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7, shared ground in both traditions, and on Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15. Historic, symbolic, and future readings of the vision appear in both traditions, and these notes present them side by side. Shared ground: the LORD himself cleanses and restores the priest who stands for his people.

verses.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the LORD’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet sees Joshua the high priest standing before the LORD’s angel, with Satan at his right hand to be his adversary. Arminian readers note the courtroom scene: the accuser stands where a prosecutor would stand, and the high priest stands for a people who have no defense of their own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same courtroom setting and read the accuser as a real hostile power held within the LORD’s rule. Readers in both traditions take the figure as a heavenly prosecutor, as Satan in the later Christian sense, or as both.

verses.text: The LORD said to Satan, “The LORD rebuke you, Satan! Yes, the LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers the accuser, “The LORD rebuke you, Satan!” and grounds the rebuke in his choice of Jerusalem. Arminian readers hear the LORD defending his people out of covenant love, and they read the burning stick plucked out of the fire, as in Amos 4:11, as a people rescued from judgment by mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read “the LORD who has chosen Jerusalem” as the ground of the rebuke, so the defense rests on God’s choice rather than Joshua’s worth; see the Psalms 132:13 box, and compare Deuteronomy 7:7. Jude 9 later uses similar words, “May the Lord rebuke you!”, in its own setting.

verses.text: Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and was standing before the angel.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua is clothed with filthy garments as he stands before the angel. Arminian readers see the defilement of the people and their priesthood after the exile, and they read the image as an honest confession that the priest who represents them cannot stand clean in his own right.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same defilement and note that the accuser’s charge is not denied; the answer is cleansing, not a plea of innocence. Shared ground: both traditions read the filthy garments as guilt and impurity that only the LORD can remove from his servant.

verses.text: He answered and spoke to those who stood before him, saying, “Take the filthy garments off him.” To him he said, “Behold, I have caused your iniquity to pass from you, and I will clothe you with rich clothing.”
verses.arminianNotes: The angel commands those who stand before him to take off the filthy garments, then tells Joshua, “Behold, I have caused your iniquity to pass from you, and I will clothe you with rich clothing.” Arminian readers see free forgiveness received by a priest who brings nothing but need, compare Isaiah 61:10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD acting entirely on Joshua’s behalf: others remove the garments, and the LORD provides the new clothing. Many Christian readers in both traditions hear an image of forgiveness and justification; on faith and justification, see the Galatians 2:16 box.

verses.text: I said, “Let them set a clean turban on his head.” So they set a clean turban on his head, and clothed him; and the LORD’s angel was standing by.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet himself speaks, asking that a clean turban be set on Joshua’s head, and it is done while the LORD’s angel stands by. Arminian readers see the prophet eagerly joining in the work of restoration, and they note that the turban recalls the high priest’s headdress described in Exodus 28.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the turban restores Joshua to his office, and some link it with the gold plate engraved “HOLY TO THE LORD” in Exodus 28:36, though that link is uncertain. Shared ground: the cleansing is complete, from garments to head covering.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel solemnly assured Joshua, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s angel solemnly assures Joshua, introducing a formal charge. Arminian readers note that the cleansing comes first and the charge follows, so the call to obedience is addressed to someone already forgiven and restored, and they hear the solemn tone as fitting a real responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the order, grace before charge, and read the solemn assurance as the LORD binding himself to his word. Shared ground: both traditions read the charge as the shape of restored service, not as the price of the cleansing given in 3:4.

verses.text: “The LORD of Armies says: ‘If you will walk in my ways, and if you will follow my instructions, then you also shall judge my house, and shall also keep my courts, and I will give you a place of access among these who stand by.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies sets conditions: if Joshua walks in his ways and follows his instructions, he will judge the LORD’s house, keep his courts, and have access among those who stand by. Arminian readers stress that the conditions are real, so Joshua’s continued privilege depends on faithful walking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the conditions are real and read them as the means by which God governs his servant’s faithfulness; compare the Philippians 2:12 box. Both traditions hold grace and responsibility together here, and access among those who stand by is often read as access to the heavenly court.

verses.text: Hear now, Joshua the high priest, you and your fellows who sit before you, for they are men who are a sign; for, behold, I will bring out my servant, the Branch.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD addresses Joshua and his fellows as men who are a sign and promises, “I will bring out my servant, the Branch.” Arminian readers note the Davidic Branch of Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 and the related imagery of Isaiah 11:1, with 2 Samuel 7 as shared ground, and they see the priests as a sign that the promise is coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same Davidic background and compare Zechariah 6:12, “the man whose name is the Branch”. Readers in both traditions see a near reference to Zerubbabel, of David’s line (1 Chronicles 3:17–19), and many also hold a Christian messianic reading, without merging the two.

verses.text: For, behold, the stone that I have set before Joshua: on one stone are seven eyes; behold, I will engrave its inscription,’ says the LORD of Armies, ‘and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks of a stone set before Joshua with seven eyes and an inscription he will engrave, and promises to remove the iniquity of that land in one day. Arminian readers note the range of readings: a temple foundation stone, a stone for the high priest’s turban, or a symbol of the Messiah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same range and link the seven eyes with “the LORD’s eyes” in 4:10, and some compare Revelation 5:6. The one day is read by some as a Day of Atonement image and by many Christians as pointing to the cross; these identifications remain uncertain in both traditions.

verses.text: In that day,’ says the LORD of Armies, ‘you will invite every man his neighbor under the vine and under the fig tree.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies promises that in that day each will invite his neighbor under the vine and under the fig tree. Arminian readers hear the peace and security of Micah 4:4 and 1 Kings 4:25, a community restored to fellowship, and they read it as the fruit of the cleansing promised in 3:9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same picture of peace and read it as the gift that follows the removal of iniquity. Readers in both traditions take it of the restored land, of the peace of the gospel, or of the final kingdom, and that difference does not follow Arminian and Reformed lines.
